solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, answers clash); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Fancy President will squash this law

indicators.note: the two words squash the law's name between them, so it sits inside the run of letters across them

explanation.surface: A dressy head of state will crush a piece of legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will squash' tells you the answer is pressed inside 'Fancy President', straddling the gap between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Cy-près is a legal doctrine letting a court apply a charitable gift as near as possible to the donor's intent.

clue.text: Cold girl I term almost 'highbrow'?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a lass is a girl

indicators.note: almost means the word for term loses its final letter

parts.note: to call something is to term it, to give it a name

explanation.surface: A frosty young woman calls herself something nearly intellectual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims CALL to CAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Classical music is the kind loosely thought of as highbrow, serious rather than popular.

clue.text: All chap mentions confuses detective

indicators.note: confuses tells us the letters of the three preceding words are jumbled up

explanation.surface: Everything a fellow says leaves a sleuth baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confuses' shuffles ALL CHAP MENTIONS into the three-word answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain-clothes officer is a police detective who works out of uniform.

clue.text: Version of text seen as incitement to rebellion, wanting leader ousted

indicators.note: the first letter of the word for stirring up revolt is pushed out

parts.note: sedition is speech or action that incites rebellion

explanation.surface: A rewritten text is judged seditious because it tells people to topple their ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting leader ousted' removes the S at the front of SEDITION.
explanation.definitionFit: An edition is one particular published version of a book or text.

clue.text: Impostor to try to make attempt at phoning Buckingham Palace?

parts.words: try to make attempt at phoning
parts.note: to ring someone is to try calling them on the telephone
Buckingham Palace is home to the monarch, abbreviated ER (Elizabeth Regina)

explanation.surface: A fraudster tries to get through by telephone to the royal household.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina; the question mark flags the palace standing for its resident.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringer is slang for a fraudulent substitute, such as a horse raced under another's name.

clue.text: Someone unwell at home with a covering, very restricted

parts.note: in means at home, as in 'staying in'
very cut down to its abbreviation, V
a lid is a covering

explanation.surface: A sick person stays indoors under a blanket, barely allowed to move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very restricted' means very reduced to its single-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An invalid is a person made weak or disabled by illness.

clue.text: An announcement that court action will proceed no further

definitions.text: An announcement that court action will proceed no further

parts.words: An announcement that court action will proceed no further
parts.note: sounds like a lawsuit being dropped, but the court is a tennis court and the call ends the contest

explanation.surface: A legal statement that a case is being halted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court action' suggests litigation; it is play on a tennis court, finished by the umpire's closing call.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is what a tennis umpire announces when the final point decides the whole contest.

clue.text: Bloomers almost break — what's inside is extraordinarily large

indicators.note: says what goes into the middle of the shortened word
almost drops the last letter of the word for a break

parts.note: a rest is a break
OS is the abbreviation for outsize, clothing that is unusually large

explanation.surface: Underwear nearly splits because the wearer inside is huge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims a break by one letter and 'what's inside is' fills it; OS (outsize) is a clothing-size label. Bloomers are any flowers here, not knickers.
explanation.definitionFit: Roses are flowers, and anything that blooms can be called a bloomer in crosswords.

clue.text: Renowned rider always in race, first and last

indicators.note: in places the word for always between the chosen letters
first and last picks the opening and closing letters of race

parts.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: A famous jockey is forever competing, winning and coming last.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Revere is the American patriot famed for his 1775 midnight ride warning of British troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Revere is celebrated for his midnight horseback ride before the battles of Lexington and Concord.

clue.text: Conspirator is a beast — American not English

indicators.note: not says the letter for English is replaced by the American one

parts.note: a brute is a beast

explanation.surface: A plotter is called an animal, and it's an American rather than an English one.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the E of BRUTE for US.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Brutus was one of the plotters who assassinated Julius Caesar.

clue.text: What draws a diner ultimately into a bad habit?

definitions.text: What draws a diner ultimately into a bad habit?

indicators.note: into says the short piece goes inside the vice

parts.note: a vice is a bad habit

indicators.note: ultimately takes the last letter of diner

explanation.surface: Asks what tempts an eater into a harmful habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' takes the diner's last letter and 'into' slips it with A inside the bad habit; the whole clue also describes greed.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed is the urge that might lure a diner into overindulgence, one of the deadly sins.

clue.text: With revolutions all around, a politician brightens up

indicators.note: all around says the revolutions enclose the other pieces

parts.note: revs are engine revolutions
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Amid sweeping change, a lawmaker livens things up.
explanation.definitionFit: To revamp something is to renovate or freshen it, giving it new life.

clue.text: Manliness? Test it out — this lot are very soppy

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the preceding words being thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone proposes testing machismo, and a group shows itself to be terribly wet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges MANLINESS TEST IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentimentalists indulge in tender emotion to excess, so a group of them is mawkish or soft.

clue.text: They've come down together — they'll be in the kitchen

parts.note: co- as a prefix means together, as in co-operate
landers are craft that have touched down, like a lunar lander

explanation.surface: People who have descended as a group will end up cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as CO-LANDERS, joint arrivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Colanders are perforated bowls used for draining food, standard kitchen equipment.

clue.text: Get rid of irritating pain after day

indicators.note: after places the irritation behind the day's letter

parts.note: an itch is an irritating sensation

explanation.surface: Banish an annoying ache once the day is done.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to discard or abandon it.

clue.text: Like an accident that could be nasty and hurting, not good

indicators.note: nasty tells us the letters are rearranged into something unpleasant
not removes the letter for good from hurting

explanation.surface: A crash that could be vicious and cause injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not good' drops G from HURTING; 'nasty' shuffles AND HURTIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A hit-and-run collision is one where the driver strikes someone and flees the scene.

clue.text: Instruments offering greetings with the Salvation Army coming out

indicators.note: coming out removes the army's letters from the greetings

parts.note: salutes are greetings
SA is the abbreviation for the Salvation Army

explanation.surface: A brass band offers welcomes as the Salvation Army marches out.
explanation.walkthrough: SALUTES loses its opening SA.
explanation.definitionFit: Lutes are plucked stringed musical instruments with a pear-shaped body.

clue.text: New-style jeans so OK for an American city

indicators.note: a new style for the letters means they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fresh look in denim is fine for a US town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New-style' rearranges JEANS SO.
explanation.definitionFit: San Jose is a large city in California, at the heart of Silicon Valley.

clue.text: Fatty seen floundering? This may prevent dangerous mishap

indicators.note: floundering suggests the letters thrashing about into a new order

explanation.surface: A heavy person is spotted struggling, and something might stop a nasty accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'floundering' rearranges FATTY SEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A safety net is stretched under acrobats to catch a falling performer, preventing serious injury.

clue.text: Reluctant to limit awful din or rumpus

indicators.note: to limit means to hem in, so the shy word encloses the rest

parts.note: shy means reluctant, as in 'shy of doing'

indicators.note: awful signals the letters of din are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is unwilling to curb a terrible noise or commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges din and 'to limit' puts the result inside the word for reluctant.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindy is an informal word for a noisy disturbance or brawl.

clue.text: Religious institution enables the young to absorb uplifting atmosphere

indicators.note: to absorb means taking something in, so the youngsters contain the next piece

parts.note: fry are young fish, and by extension young children

indicators.note: uplifting in a down clue sends the word read bottom to top

parts.note: air is atmosphere

explanation.surface: A church body helps youngsters soak up an inspiring mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplifting' reverses the atmosphere in this down clue, and 'to absorb' puts it inside the young, who are called fry like young fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A friary is a community house where friars live, a religious establishment.

clue.text: Author in sort of depression, upset over a trifle

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the slot upside down, reading it bottom to top

parts.note: a slot is a kind of narrow hollow
a toy is a trifle, a thing of little value

explanation.surface: A writer is depressed, distressed over something trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses the depression; in a down clue 'over' means it sits above the trifle.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo Tolstoy was the Russian novelist who wrote War and Peace.

clue.text: Short novel featuring one in evil banishment abroad

indicators.note: abroad means scattered widely, so these letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A brief book about someone wickedly sent into exile overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' rearranges I, EVIL and BANISHMENT; H. G. Wells's tale is a novella.
explanation.definitionFit: H. G. Wells's 1897 book about a scientist who becomes unseen is a short novel.

clue.text: Walk — ploy to catch maiden

indicators.note: to catch means to hold, so the ploy encloses the letter

parts.note: a trap is a ploy, a trick
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A stroll turns out to be a trick for snaring a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily or a long way on foot.

clue.text: A member can't take more than this

definitions.text: A member can't take more than this

parts.words: A member can't take more than this
parts.note: member seems a club member, but it is a limb, and the clue describes the most it can carry

explanation.surface: A society member has reached a limit on what they can accept.
explanation.definitionFit: An armload is the quantity a single limb can carry, so a 'member' read as a limb holds no more.

clue.text: One goes around a hill confronted by rubbish

indicators.note: confronted by places the rubbish in front of the hill

parts.note: rot means rubbish, nonsense
a tor is a rocky hill, common in Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Someone circles a hill littered with garbage.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotator is something that turns or revolves, such as a muscle or machine part.

clue.text: Dramatist and unmarried woman — no saints

indicators.note: no means the saints are removed from the word

parts.note: a spinster is an unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A playwright and a single woman, neither of them holy.
explanation.walkthrough: SPINSTER loses both its S letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter was a British playwright, author of The Birthday Party.

clue.text: Snake? It's surprisingly not used by nasty hypnotist

indicators.note: surprisingly signals the letters are mixed
not used by says the letters of the first words are left out of the mix

explanation.surface: A sinister mesmerist surprisingly doesn't use a reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ITS out of HYPNOTIST; 'surprisingly' shuffles HYPNOT into the snake.
explanation.definitionFit: A python is a large constricting snake of Africa, Asia and Australia.
